blocks.text: Alkhabeer Diversified Income Traded Fund (“the Fund”) is a closed-ended Shari’a-compliant investment traded fund established in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and regulated by the Capital Market Authority (CMA). The Fund’s investment objective is to generate periodic income to investors by investing in Shari’a-compliant income generating assets. The Fund Manager “Alkhabeer Capital” plans to invest in Sukuk, trade finance transactions, leasing transactions, income funds and Murabaha transactions, either directly or through investment funds.

4. Standard Deviation is a measure of risk. It is calculated as any volatility in returns over a period of time. The lower the volatility, the more homogeneous the set of returns.
5. Sharpe Ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure. It is calculated as the difference as the Fund Manager excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by the Standard Deviation. The greater a portfolio's Sharpe Ratio, the better its risk-adjusted performance.
6. Tracking Error is a measure of risk. It is calculated as the Standard Deviation between the Fund Manager's returns and the Benchmark's returns. The lower the Tracking Error, the lower the Fund Manager deviates from the Benchmark.
7. Beta is a measure of the average historical sensitivity of the Fund's returns compared to market returns. It is calculated by using the covariance of the Fund and the market on the variance of the market.
8. Alpha measures any excess return achieved by the Fund compared to the performance of the index.
9. Information Ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure. It is calculated as the active return of the Fund Manager, divided by its tracking error. The higher the Information ratio, the higher the Fund Manager ability to generate excess returns per Unit of excess risk. Knowing that the performance and risk parameters were calculated based on the Unit's trading prices in the market.
FUND HIGHLIGHTS AND ANY FUNDAMENTAL, OR NON-FUNDAMENTAL CHANGES AFFECTING THE PERFORMANCE OF THE FUND

items: The Fund Manager invested 34.4% of the Fund’s assets in leasing transactions across several types of equipment and companies. The leasing portfolio is mainly invested in the United States and is expected to generate a total return of 6.0% to 6.5% annually over the next five-year term.

To diversify the Fund’s investments, the Fund Manager invested 23.8% of the Fund’s assets in income funds, ranging between private financing, trade finance and securitization, with an expected average annual return of 6.0% to 7.0%.

The Fund Manager invested 20.4% of the Fund’s assets in trade finance transactions with several counterparties and across various industries, mostly in the European continent. All executed transactions are of a short-term nature, with returns ranging between 6.0% to 7.0% annually.

The Fund Manager invested 12.2% of the Fund’s assets in Sukuk of different credit ratings, including sovereign, quasi-sovereign and corporate Sukuk. The Fund Manager has obtained credit facilities that support increasing the Portfolio’s returns to over 4.5% per annum, while maintaining a weighted average for classifying the Portfolio as an investment grade.

blocks.text: OVERVIEW OF THE LEASING, TRADE FINANCE AND SUKUK INDUSTRIES

Rising interest rate situation, the pandemic overhang, and severe supply chain bottlenecks have pushed for a greater need in the equipment financing industry. Meanwhile, the Equipment Leasing & Finance Foundation’s Monthly Confidence Index (MCI-EFI) stood at 50.9 in June, almost steady with the May index of 49.6. A reading above 50 indicates a positive business outlook. It is anticipated that the US equipment and software investment to expand by 4.2% in 2022. However, it is also expected that the pace of investment will slow before improving modestly during the second half of the year. The Fund Manager trusts that the ongoing increase in interest rates would support the financial health of the equipment finance companies as obligors would adopt to the new world rate order and margins would be built back in the markets.

items: Rising commodity prices in consequence to Russia-Ukraine war and COVID-19 containment measures in East Asia placed further pressure on the prices of traded goods and on already strained supply chains.

As per Fitch Ratings, the biggest European commodity trade finance banks including Société Générale, ING, Rabobank, Crédit Agricole, Groupe BPCE and UBS already appear to be growing their lending to commodity trading companies amid unprecedented liquidity needs. As per the agency, record high commodity prices have induced increased margin requirements from central clearing counterparties and in turn, have led to higher demand for financing among commodity traders.

The Boston Consulting Group (BCG) also notes that surge in prices of most key commodities including not only oil and gas but also soft commodities such as wheat is creating a larger revenue opportunity for trade finance market players.
The Fund Manager believes that the higher demand for financing will allow Trade Finance firms to improve their level of profitability.

Global Sukuk issuance had a stronger start in 2022, building on considerable momentum it had built up in 2021. According to Refinitiv, total Sukuk issuance reached a total of $51.6 billion in Q1 2022, compared to $43.4 billion issued in Q1 2021.

Notably, the boost in Q1 issuance came from Sukuk issued by Saudi Arabian entities, which almost doubled from $9.3 billion in Q1 2021 to $17.9 billion in Q1 2022, outpacing the Sukuk issued by market leader Malaysia for the first time.

The Fund Manager anticipates the Sukuk market to remain robust in the long term maintained by issuances from net oil importing sovereign issuers. Important stock of upcoming debt maturities and funding diversification strategies will also support this asset class.
